context: A class of learners in which some play football, some play hockey and some play both sports.
stem: In a class, ${=f}$ learners play football and ${=h}$ learners play hockey. ${=c}$ learners play both sports. The numbers for football and for hockey each include the learners who play both. How many learners play football or hockey (or both)?
solution: Draw a Venn diagram with two overlapping circles, $F$ for football and $H$ for hockey. The overlap holds the ${=c}$ learners who play both.
Football only: ${=f} - {=c} = {=f - c}$. Hockey only: ${=h} - {=c} = {=h - c}$.
Add the three regions: ${=f - c} + {=c} + {=h - c} = {=u}$, so ${=u}$ learners play football or hockey (or both).
The identity gives the same result: $n(F \text{ or } H) = n(F) + n(H) - n(F \text{ and } H) = {=f} + {=h} - {=c} = {=u}$.
notes: Entry point of the skill (the book has no basic question here): one use of the union identity, checked against the Venn regions. The stem states that the football and hockey totals include those who play both, so a blind solver cannot read them as 'only' counts; the book leaves this implicit in ex14-8-30. The misconception catalogue for this objective is empty and this is a numeric family, so no distractors or misconception ids are used. Common slip a reviewer may want catalogued: adding f + h and forgetting to subtract the overlap (double counting). Instance range: f 10-25, h 8-22, c 3 to min(f, h) - 3, so every region is non-empty.
